title: Exploration
section: The outcome on its own
text:
The outcome on its own
Getting the baseline: what does delivery days look like at Olist?


Code
df_master_clean |>
  summarise(
    min_del_days = min(delivery_days),
    avg_del_days = mean(delivery_days),
    median_del_days = median(delivery_days),
    max_del_days = max(delivery_days),
    sd_del_days = sd(delivery_days),
    num_orders = n_distinct(order_id)
  )


# A tibble: 1 × 6
  min_del_days avg_del_days median_del_days max_del_days sd_del_days num_orders
         <dbl>        <dbl>           <dbl>        <dbl>       <dbl>      <int>
1            0         12.0              10          209        9.45      96476


The mean sits above the median, so delivery days are skewed to the right, with the right tail going up to a maximum of 209 days. Every comparison from here is judged against this baseline.

title: Exploration
section: Data manipulations
text:
Data manipulations
Adding the following calculated fields 1. Time- based - Weekday/weekend flag based on the day of the week - hour of day (based on timestamp) - time of day (morning, afternoon, evening or night time)


Code
library(lubridate) # Used to extract time based features from timestamp

df_master_clean <- df_master_clean |>
  mutate(
    hour_of_day = hour(order_purchase_timestamp),
    day_type = case_when(
      purchase_day_of_week %in% c("Saturday", "Sunday") ~ "Weekend",
      TRUE ~ "Weekday"),
    time_of_day = case_when(
      hour_of_day < 6 ~ "night",
      hour_of_day < 12 ~ "morning",
      hour_of_day < 17 ~ "afternoon",
      hour_of_day < 21 ~ "evening",
      TRUE ~ "night"
    )
  )

Heavier items cost more to ship, but weight explains only part of freight. Weekday vs. weekend makes no difference.

title: Exploration
section: What the exploration says about the business question
text:
What the exploration says about the business question

Delivery performance is strong overall. About 90% of orders arrive earlier than estimated, so Olist’s estimates are conservative. - Delivery days and total cost are both right skewed, with a small tail of very slow or very expensive orders.
When you order barely matters. Weekday v/s weekend and time of day show similar delivery status shares and delivery time distributions, so purchase timing is not a meaningful driver of delays.
Geography and product type matter more. Delivery time varies by customer state (Amapá and Roraima slowest, São Paulo fastest) and by category (office furniture slowest, likely tied to its heavy average weight).
Heavier items cost more to ship. Freight rises with product weight, though with wide spread, and freight value is modestly related to delivery days.

title: Home
section: Why this matters
text:
Why this matters
Olist is a Brazilian online marketplace that connects small sellers to customers across the country. Delivery speed and shipping cost are central to customer satisfaction, and they are set by logistics: where the seller and customer are, how heavy the item is, and what category it belongs to. About two years of order data (2016-2018) can show where the delivery promise holds, where it breaks, and what drives shipping costs.
Use the navbar: Data and Exploration are the analysis, covering the order-level dataset (about 110K item rows), the calculated fields I built (delivery status, total cost, time-of-day features), and the plots that compare delivery time, freight, weight, and category. The remaining pages cover the file format, the presentation slides, and the GitHub and Netlify setup.

About 90% of orders arrive earlier than estimated, so Olist’s delivery estimates are conservative.
Purchase timing (weekday vs. weekend, time of day) barely changes delivery outcomes.
Location and product type matter more: delivery time varies by customer state and by category, and heavier items cost more to ship.

df_master <- df_master |>
  rename(
    product_name_length = product_name_lenght,
    product_description_length = product_description_lenght
  ) |>
  mutate(
    purchase_year_month = make_date(purchase_year, purchase_month, 1)
  ) |>
  filter(!is.na(delivery_days))

rows_after_target_filter <- nrow(df_master)

df_master <- df_master |>
  mutate(
    product_category_name = if_else(is.na(product_category_name), "unknown", product_category_name),
    product_category_name_english = if_else(
      is.na(product_category_name_english),
      product_category_name,
      product_category_name_english
    ),
    across(
      c(
        product_name_length,
        product_description_length,
        product_photos_qty,
        product_weight_g,
        product_length_cm,
        product_height_cm,
        product_width_cm
      ),
      ~ if_else(is.na(.x), median(.x, na.rm = TRUE), .x)
    )
  )




Summary of Cleaning Decisions (One Sentence per Rule)

Column name & date standardization: Corrected the raw typos (product_name_lenght -> product_name_length and product_description_lenght -> product_description_length) and built purchase_year_month so naming is consistent and monthly trends can be tracked cleanly.
Missing target removal: Removed 2,454 rows (2.18%) missing delivery_days—moving from 112,650 to 110,196 rows—because records without an observed delivery duration cannot train or evaluate a delivery_days model.
Category missingness ("unknown"): Filled missing product_category_name and product_category_name_english entries with "unknown" rather than dropping rows so uncategorized items still contribute shipping, timing, and geographic records.
Numeric product spec imputation (median): Imputed missing values across the seven numeric product specification columns (product_name_length, product_description_length, product_photos_qty, product_weight_g, product_length_cm, product_height_cm, and product_width_cm) using each column’s median because product dimensions and counts are skewed and the median resists extreme outliers.

After cleaning, 0 missing values remain across all 34 columns in 110,196 rows (96,476 unique orders).
